messages.author: f2777afe52b659e4
messages.subject: ice on transect ?
parts:
Hi,

what should one do if there is a varying amount of ice on the line
transect (e.g. boat-based), making specific but unknown transect areas
unavailable ?

Ideally, one could fly over the transect afterwards, take a picture of
the survey area, and subtract the iced area.
However, in reality that's usually impossible. Sometimes, ice floats
very fast, too, and modifies the image.

For now, I would treat surveys from such areas as underestimates since
the transect area assigned to corrected bird numbers is smaller than
what is used for the computation. I am unclear about the variance
though.

Thanks for any advice; best regards

F.

Falk Huettmann

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: ice on transect ?
parts:
I presume you mean that it is unuseable in the sense that D=0 in the
ice-covered areas. If that is the case, you use the entire transect
length and the entire area of the survey region. Average D will be
lower but with a proper design it will be unbiased for the entire region
and total abundance estimator will be unbiased. However, the estimated
D is not an estimate of density in useable area, but is it really
necessary? It isn't needed to estimate abundance!

Now if what you are saying is that the critter is under the ice, then
you have a different problem.

--jeff

messages.author: 4c1c72aa70d13107
messages.subject: Re: ice on transect ?
parts:
Rod's caveats brings up some interesting points about 1.) stratification
and 2.) heterogeneity in detection probability. I hope to hear more
discussion. Somebody steer me back on course.

1.) Stratification by areas with more ice, even if it is 8/10 of the
length, is not necessary. That is, estimates are unbiased. However
stratification may, under some circumstances, increase precision.
Specifically, this will only be a large benefit when lines vary in the
amount of ice they traverse. Perhaps a ratio estimator would perform
better anyway(?) - in which case you are back to simply exluding the ice
areas and using shortened line lengths. Why stratify?

2.) The second and third concerns listed by Rod (whether ice affect
detectability through sighting conditions or animal behavior) are factors
that induce heterogeneity in individual detection probability. "Pooling
robustness" or approximate robustness should negate this as a critical
concern (?). Assuming there is no sample bias (eg, to avoid ice edges) I
do not see any problem if ice does indeed affect animal behavior or
detectability. These factors are already highly variable across a study
area anyway. It seems to me that pooling robustness is not well
understood, myself included. Can anyone provide some insight?

These are difficulties that I often hear about in designing distance
surveys, and I think many of them are unnecessary. Specifically, the
properties of random samples and pooling robust modeling allow for our
ignorance every possible factor affecting density or detectability. Any
thoughts?

Cheers,
~aaron

I agree with Jeff that if the ice represents random patches of zero
density
then you should be able to proceed with the analysis, ignoring the ice.
However, you should consider the possible impact of ice on the survey,
for
instance:
1) Did ice impact the survey design? Not just dodging the occasional
berg
but say your survey tracks were all <3/10 ice but your study area
included
8/10 ice then you may need to stratify your data.
2) Does the ice affect the observations? By creating visual contrast or
acting as cue.
3) Do the birds behave differently in the area around ice or in
different
densities of ice? e.g. resting on or near ice and foraging in open
water.

Rod

messages.subject: Re: ice on transect ?
parts:
Aaron, I've pasted below text from the upcoming advanced distance sampling
book on pooling robustness. (The book is now in press.) Apologies for
the unreadable Latex'ed equations - but the text covers some of your
queries.

Steve

\section{Pooling robustness}
\label{ads_misc_pooling_robust}

Burnham {\it et al.}\ (1980) introduced the important concept of pooling
robustness. They noted that detectability depends on many factors other
than just distance from the line or point. Some of these factors are
internal, such as age, sex or size of the animal, or cluster size if
animals occur in clusters. Others are external, such as weather,
visibility, habitat, observer or observation platform. Because data are
rarely adequate to allow stratification by more than one or two factors,
Burnham {\it et al.}\ (1980) note the importance of using models that
yield unbiased (or nearly unbiased) estimates when distance data collected
under variable conditions and on animals with varying intrinsic
detectabilities are pooled. We explore here the issue of pooling
robustness.

In Chapter \ref{ads_cov}, we provide methods that allow covariates to be
included in the model for detectability. These methods reduce the reliance
on pooling robustness, although they do not remove it altogether, as we
cannot be sure that we have the right covariates, entering our model in
the right form. The methods also allow the user to explore how
detectability varies as covariates vary. Another advantage of modelling
the covariates is when separate estimates are needed of different
components of the population, such as males and females. If we just pool
the data across the sexes when detectability varies by sex, pooling
robustness provides an estimate of total population size with low bias
(unless one sex is much more detectable than the other --- see below), but
the separate estimates of males and females may be appreciably
biased. Addition of sex as a factor with two levels overcomes this
difficulty. However, the results of this section show that, if only an
overall abundance estimate is required, standard methods without
covariates are satisfactory under rather mild conditions, provided
heterogeneity in detectability is not too extreme.

Burnham {\it et al.}\ (1980: 45) consider partitioning line transect data
into $r$ strata, chosen so that there is little heterogeneity with each
stratum. The pooling robustness criterion is then defined as
\begin{equation}
\label{ach11_robust_criterion}
n\hat{f}(0) = \sum^r _{j=1} n_j \hat{f}_j(0)
\end{equation}
where $n_j$ is the number of detections in stratum $j$, $\hat{f}_j(0)$ is
the corresponding fitted pdf of distances of detected objects from the
line evaluated at zero distance, $n$ is the total number of detections,
and $\hat{f}(0)$ is the pdf fitted to the pooled distance data, evaluated
at zero distance.

In the following, we assume that animals occur singly; if they do not,
then each reference to `animal' below should be read as `cluster'.

Using the notation of Chapter \ref{ads_cov}, $y$ is distance from the line
or point, $\underline{z}$ are the covariates associated with an animal,
$g(y,\underline{z})$ is the probability of detection of an animal at
distance $y$ from the line or point and with covariate values
$\underline{z}$, and $f(y,\underline{z})$ is the corresponding joint
density function.

We make two key assumptions here:
\begin{enumerate}
\item{$g(0,\underline{z})=1$ for all $\underline{z}$}
\item{$\pi(y,\underline{z})=\pi(y)\pi(\underline{z})$, the product of the
marginals}
\end{enumerate}
Random line or point placement, or more usually random placement of a
systematic grid of lines or points, ensures independence of $y$ and
$\underline{z}$, so that the second assumption holds.

From eqn (\ref{ach3_joint_density}),
\begin{equation}
f(y,\underline{z}) = \frac{g(y,\underline{z}) \, \pi(y) \,
\pi(\underline{z})}{\int\int g(y,\underline{z}) \,\pi(y) \,
\pi(\underline{z}) \, dy \, d\underline{z}}
\end{equation}

The marginal density of $y$ is therefore
\begin{equation}
f(y) = \frac{\int g(y,\underline{z}) \, \pi(y) \,
\pi(\underline{z})\,d\underline{z}}{\int\int
g(y,\underline{z}) \,\pi(y) \, \pi(\underline{z}) \, dy \, d\underline{z}}
\label{ach11_marginal}
\end{equation}

The probability that an animal at distance $y$ is detected, unconditional
on $\underline{z}$, is
\begin{equation}
g(y)=\int g(y,\underline{z})\,\pi(\underline{z})\, d\underline{z}
\end{equation}

Hence eqn (\ref{ach11_marginal}) simplifies to
\begin{equation}
f(y) = \frac{g(y) \, \pi(y)}{\int g(y) \,\pi(y) \, dy}
\end{equation}

For line transect sampling, given random line placement,
$\pi(y)=\frac{1}{w}$, so that
\begin{equation}
f(y) = \frac{g(y)}{\int g(y) \, dy}
\end{equation}
whereas for point transect sampling, we have $\pi(y)=\frac{2y}{w^2}$ and
\begin{equation}
f(y) = \frac{y\,g(y)}{\int y\,g(y) \, dy}
\end{equation}

These are exactly the results that apply in the absence of
heterogeneity. This is sufficient to show that the two sides of eqn
(\ref{ach11_robust_criterion}) have the same large-sample expectation; the
pooling robustness criterion can be assumed to hold provided we have a
sufficiently flexible model for $g(y)$ to fit to the observed distance
data.

The implications of these results are perhaps surprising. For example, the
training of shipboard observers often includes a warning that they should
maintain constant search effort. If observers search less efficiently in
areas of low density through boredom, and more efficiently when they are
in areas of high density, then the effective strip width is systematically
greater in high-density areas and less elsewhere. This was thought to
generate bias in abundance estimates, whereas the above results show that
it does not --- so long as they maintain $g(0)=1$ in both high and low
density areas. We would like observers to search with high efficiency
throughout, as a larger number of detections gives higher precision, but
abundance estimation is not compromised if efficiency is variable.

In Section \ref{ach11_cont_hr_models}, the hazard-rate model
$g(y)=1-exp[-(y/\sigma)^{-b}]$ was derived from homogeneous models for the
sighting process. In Fig.\ 11.2, composite detection functions were shown
when there is heterogeneity in detection probabilities. Although the
hazard-rate detection function has a
flat shoulder followed by a steep fall-off, the composite detection
function has a rounded
shoulder, more like that of the half-normal model. This illustrates that,
to utilize the model-robustness properties of line transect estimators, it
is important to use flexible models that can change shape when data
arising from different detection functions are pooled.

If heterogeneity is sufficiently extreme, it becomes difficult to model
adequately the detection function close to zero. For example in some
shipboard surveys, one or more observers search through $20\times$ or
$25\times$
binoculars, while another observer `guards the trackline' by searching
with the naked eye. If $g(0)$ is appreciably less than one for the main
observers, the detection function may appear to have a shoulder, but with
a spike of observations at around zero distance from the line (Fig.\ 2.1
of Buckland {\it et al}.\ (2001: 31)). Another example would be a species
of songbird, for which males are almost certain to be detected out to
perhaps 50 m or more, whereas females beyond perhaps 5 m may avoid
detection. This degree
of heterogeneity cannot be reliably modelled, resulting in bias.

Given assumption 1, that $g(0,\underline{z})=1$, then $g(0)=\int
g(0,\underline{z})\,\pi(\underline{z})\, d\underline{z} = 1$. If
$g(0,\underline{z})$ is a function of $\underline{z}$, then the model
robustness criterion fails, and we must model the heterogeneity to avoid
bias (Chapter \ref{ads_g(0)}).

Link (2003) noted the unidentifiability that can occur in estimating
population size using mark-recapture, when there is heterogeneity in the
capture probabilities. In the last sentence of that article, he stated
that `similar difficulties are to be anticipated in the use of distance
sampling models ..., in which inference is based on a density value at
zero.' The results of this section demonstrate that this is not true,
provided $g(0,\underline{z})=1$ for all $\underline{z}$. In
mark-recapture, to estimate population size, a model is needed that allows
estimation of the number of animals that are never caught, and different
models may give very different estimates. Mark-recapture data are discrete
counts of animals with different capture histories, and from these, we
must attempt to estimate the frequency of the `never caught' capture
history. By contrast, in line transect sampling, we seek to estimate
$f(0)$, the pdf of detection distances at zero distance, by fitting a
smooth, continuous function to $f(y)$. Under rather mild assumptions
(principally that $g(0,\underline{z})=1$ and that $g'(0,\underline{z})=0$
for all $\underline{z}$), the method works well. Similar arguments apply
in point transect sampling, where estimation of $h(0)$ relies on a good
model for the slope of the pdf at zero distance.
